How Does a Single Shot Become a World War? · Simulatio Lab
See how far a small clash spreads depending on how dense the alliances are and how strictly pacts are honored, using an abstract cascade model.
All experiments

When one country attacks another, its allies are drawn in one by one. Sometimes it ends with two or three countries; sometimes nearly every country is entangled. At what point does that difference appear as alliances thicken? This is an abstract toy model with 24 anonymous countries, and it does not explain the causes of any real war.
How the model works
There are 24 countries (A–X). If two countries are allies, one gets a call for help when the other enters a war. Alliances are mutual-aid pacts, and the countries are anonymous, with no names or map.

Choose one of three alliance structures: random (an average number of allies per country), two blocs (alliances inside each bloc, with 2 links between blocs), or isolated pairs (each country has exactly one ally).

At the start one country (the red side) attacks another (the blue side). Each round, every neutral country is pulled in by each of its allies already at war with the probability "chance an ally honors the pact." If it is called from both sides at once, it goes to the side with more calls, and picks randomly on a tie.

The war ends when no new country joins. On this page, a war that pulls in half of all countries (12) or more is called "world-war scale," and 4 countries or fewer is "stayed small." These cutoffs are for explanation only.

What This Shows, and What It Doesn't

What it shows: In this model, with the same 24 countries and the same pacts, once alliances got reasonably dense a small clash suddenly spread to nearly every country. At a 70% chance of honoring pacts, with an average of 0 allies per country the war always ended with 2 countries; with 1 ally it averaged 6.3 countries (world-war scale 15%), 1.5 allies 12.1 (56%), 2 allies 17.4 (85%), 3 allies 22.4 (99%), and with 4 or more nearly every country was drawn in. Even with 3 allies on average, a 10% chance of honoring pacts gave 4.0 countries on average (world-war scale 6%) and 30% gave 16.0 (71%). With isolated pairs, the war stopped at 4 countries at most however strictly pacts were honored.

What it doesn't show: It does not mean real wars, or the events of 1914, unfolded like this, and it assigns responsibility to no country or leader. Real wars involve politics, economics, military planning, misunderstandings, choices and the actual content of alliances, and none of that is here. It is a very simple toy model in which countries are identical, alliances are plain links, and being "pulled in" is decided by probability alone. The average number of allies and the chance of honoring a pact are not real-world figures.
Implementation notes

This is a simple design by this project, inspired by contagion and cascade models (for example Watts (2002), "A simple model of global cascades on random networks", PNAS 99(9)). It does not reproduce a paper's model or values, and it is not historical research. The countries are anonymous A–X, with no real countries, leaders or dates.

Random alliances give every pair of countries the same chance of being allied (the average number of allies is the slider value). In two blocs, each bloc of 12 forms alliances the same way only inside the bloc, with 2 links between the blocs, and the first attack happens between different blocs. In isolated pairs, the 24 countries are matched into 12 pairs.

The figures above are averages of 400 runs of the same setting (node tools/validate-alliance.js), while graphs ③–⑤ are results of 300 runs or 6 batches of 40 on screen, so the numbers can differ slightly. In two blocs, with an average of 1 ally inside a bloc the war averaged 7.4 countries (world-war scale 22%), and with 2 allies 18.9 countries (90%).

How Do Apartment Prices Spread? · Simulatio Lab
Watch a price rise in one neighborhood spread to its neighbors, and change the loan cap and a rate shock. A toy model, not investment advice.

Does a price rise that starts in one neighborhood spread to its neighbors? Change how strongly people follow recent gains next door (price contagion), the loan cap and a rate shock, and watch 900 neighborhoods on a grid. It is a toy model of the structure, not a picture of any real area.
Each cell of a 30×30 grid is a neighborhood, and every price index starts at 100. One step is one quarter. The rise starts in the central 7×7 block (dashed square).
Each neighborhood's growth combines its own recent gains (momentum), the recent gains of its 8 neighbors (price contagion), the expectation that prices keep rising, and small random shocks.

There is an "income line" that rises slowly with incomes, and a higher loan cap lets prices climb further above it (the affordability ceiling). Above the ceiling growth is dragged down; below the line buyers return.
If you choose a rate shock, from that quarter the ceiling drops and expectations sour, so prices cool.

A toy model built on the idea of herding, being drawn by neighbors' recent gains, and on spatial diffusion models. It draws inspiration from Shiller's work on how market sentiment and narratives move prices, but it does not reproduce any specific paper or real data; it is this project's own design.

Growth = 0.30 × (own previous growth) + contagion × (average of 8 neighbors) + 0.004 × optimism + a random shock (SD 0.6%). The ceiling = income line × (loan cap ÷ 0.4)<sup>1.5</sup>; above the ceiling growth is reduced by 25% of the log gap, and below the income line it is raised by the same amount. Income grows 0.5% per quarter.

A rate shock cuts the ceiling by 30% from that quarter, reduces optimism to a quarter, and adds a downward pressure (up to −1.2%) that fades over 12 quarters. All these constants were chosen arbitrarily.

Why Does Winning an Auction Cost You? · Simulatio Lab
Run the winner's curse yourself and see why the highest bidder in a painting auction loses money on average.

Nobody knows a painting's true value, and each bidder holds a slightly wrong estimate. The highest bidder wins the auction, but is that really good news? Change the number of bidders, the estimation error and how much people shade their bids.
The painting's true value V is the same for everyone but unknown (random between 70 and 130 in each auction). Each bidder receives an estimate of V with some error added.
Everyone bids "estimate − shading × size of the error". With shading at 0, they simply bid their estimate.
The highest bid wins. The price is the winner's own bid in the first-price rule, and the second-highest bid in the second-price rule.
The winner's profit is the true value minus the price paid (values average 100). If everyone shades by the same amount, the winner stays the same and only the price drops.

What it shows: With 10 bidders and a 20% estimation error, bidding the estimate (first-price rule) gave winners an average profit of −30.9 on a value of 100, and the share of losing winners rounded to 100% out of 40,000 auctions. Winning itself means "my estimate was the highest one", which is the one most wrong in the optimistic direction. The size of the loss scales with the error: −7.7 at 5% error, −15.4 at 10% and −61.7 at 40%, always about 1.54 times the error size. More bidders make it worse: −11.4 with 2, −23.5 with 5, −30.9 with 10 and −40.9 with 30. Everyone has to shade by 1.54 error sizes for the average profit to reach 0 (1.00 in the second-price rule), and more bidders need more shading.

What it doesn't show: This does not mean winners of real art auctions always lose money. The model is a common-value auction in which everyone shares one true value; real works also carry personal taste (private value), and bidders learn from experience. The bidders here are also simple: they do not account for "winning is bad news", and the model does not compute the equilibrium bids of auction theory. It does not conclude that the second-price rule is always better either: with 2 bidders, winners made +11.3 on average under the second-price rule.

This project's own implementation illustrating the "winner's curse" described in Capen, Clapp and Campbell (1971), "Competitive bidding in high-risk situations", Journal of Petroleum Technology 23, and Thaler (1988), "The winner's curse", Journal of Economic Perspectives 2(1). It does not reproduce the numbers of either paper.

The estimation error is a normal distribution with mean 0, and its standard deviation is a percentage of the value 100. If everyone shades by the same amount, the winner does not change and the price drops by shading × standard deviation, so the average profit rises exactly linearly with shading. Graphs ③ and ④ average 3 runs of 3,000 auctions each.
You can verify with node tools/validate-auction.js. With 40,000 auctions, the break-even shading is 1.54σ in the first-price rule and 1.00σ in the second-price rule.

Why Is the Popular Restaurant Always Packed? · Simulatio Lab
Why does everyone lose when everyone thinks alike? Run the El Farol Bar problem and change how people predict.

"That place was empty last week, so I'll go this week." If everyone thinks that way, the place is jammed. If everyone thinks "It was crowded last week, so let's skip it," it's empty. How do people solve this dilemma?
100 people decide every week whether to go to the restaurant. If more than the capacity (60 by default) show up, it's crowded and everyone is unhappy; otherwise they're happy.
Everyone has a way of predicting "how many people will come this week?" Each is a formula that weights the past 8 weeks differently: some "follow last week," others "do the opposite of last week."
Each person predicts this week's crowd using whichever method has been most accurate lately, and goes if the prediction is below capacity.
In the "Everyone the same" setting, every person predicts "this week will be the same as last week."

This implements the El Farol Bar problem from W. Brian Arthur (1994), "Inductive reasoning and bounded rationality", American Economic Review 84(2). The original uses a capacity of 60 and 100 people, and so do the defaults here.

Unlike the original's list of predictors, this implementation gives each person random weighted-sum predictors, so the graphs don't look exactly like the paper's. A feature of this setup is that attendance gathers very stably around capacity.
"Chose wrongly" is judged by that week's outcome: going when it was crowded, or staying home when it was empty, counts as wrong. You can verify with node tools/validate-more.js bar.

Braess's Paradox · Simulatio Lab
Run Braess's paradox yourself: simulate drivers choosing their own routes and see why opening a shortcut can raise everyone's average commute.
A New Road Made Everyone Slower: Braess's Paradox

It is easy to think that if roads are jammed, you should build a new one: more roads should shorten everyone's commute. In this simple road network, though, opening a shortcut in front of 4,000 drivers sends them all onto it, and the average commute grows from 65 to 80 minutes. Close one road and things get faster. Nobody did anything wrong: everyone just picked the route that was fastest for them.

There are two routes from start to destination: Route A (start→A→destination) and Route B (start→B→destination). Start→A and B→destination are congestible roads: the time grows by the sensitivity for every 1,000 drivers on them (10 minutes by default, so x drivers take x/100 minutes). A→destination and start→B always take 45 minutes, however many cars use them.
Opening the shortcut adds a third route (start→A→B→destination) that crosses from A to B. Crossing takes a fixed time (0 minutes by default) and never gets congested.

Each round, 8% of drivers reconsider their route. They switch only if the time they would get after switching is clearly shorter, and they move one at a time, so the system ends where nobody can gain by switching alone.

The lowest average time reachable if a planner could assign routes in the same network is the social optimum. The selfish equilibrium's average time divided by the social optimum is the price of anarchy.

What it shows: With 4,000 drivers, a 0-minute shortcut and sensitivity 10 (x/100 minutes), the equilibrium without the shortcut split drivers evenly between Routes A and B for an average of 65.0 minutes. Once the shortcut opened, drivers drifted to it, the average reached 79.5 minutes by round 100, and by round 180 everyone (100%) used the shortcut route for an average of 80.0 minutes. At that end state, switching alone gained 0 minutes. Going the other way, closing the shortcut brought the average from 79.7 minutes just before the closure down to 65.0 minutes within 5 rounds. If everyone agreed to skip the shortcut it would be 65.0 minutes, and a planner assigning routes optimally (about 13% on the shortcut) reached 64.7, so the price of anarchy was 1.24. The effect depended on the number of drivers. Below 3,000 drivers the shortcut helped (2,000 drivers: 55.0 → 40.0 minutes), at 3,000 it was a tie at 60.0 minutes, between 3,000 and 9,000 it hurt, most at 4,500 drivers with 67.5 → 90.0 minutes (1.33 times), and from 9,000 drivers on nobody used it so nothing changed. With a shortcut cost of 25 minutes or more the result was 65.0 minutes, the same as closed, and at 5 minutes it was 85.0 minutes, worse than at 0 minutes (80.0). With congestion sensitivity 5 the shortcut helped (55.0 → 40.0 minutes), and with 20 it hurt (85.0 → 90.0 minutes).

What it doesn't show: This does not reproduce any real city's road network. It is this project's simplified model: a small symmetric network, everyone with the same origin and destination, drivers who care only about time, and the same choices repeated day after day. It does not mean shortcuts or new roads are always harmful, nor that roads should not be built: with light traffic the shortcut clearly helped. Stories from places such as Stuttgart or Seoul's Cheonggyecheon, where closing or removing a road supposedly improved traffic, are often cited as examples of this paradox, but they are mixed with other changes in traffic, so the evidence is anecdotal, and this model neither explains nor reproduces those events. Reality also involves things this model leaves out, such as switching to public transport, changing departure times, and induced demand where a new road brings new traffic.

This project's own implementation illustrating the paradox described in Braess (1968), "Über ein Paradoxon aus der Verkehrsplanung", Unternehmensforschung 12, 258-268. It does not reproduce that paper's numbers; the setting of 4,000 drivers, x/100 minutes on congestible roads and a fixed 45 minutes follows the widely used textbook example (Easley & Kleinberg, Networks, Crowds, and Markets).

Treating drivers as a continuous quantity, the equilibrium can be solved in closed form. With a = sensitivity/1000, fixed time 45 and shortcut cost c: if a × drivers + c ≤ 45 everyone takes the shortcut and the average is 2a × drivers + c; if it is more crowded but a × drivers < 2(45 − c), only some take it and all three routes tie at 90 − c; beyond that nobody takes it, same as closed. Graphs ④ and ⑤ use these formulas, and I checked that the end state of the simulation matches them.

For linear delays (a congestible road's time proportional to its drivers), Roughgarden & Tardos (2002), "How bad is selfish routing?", Journal of the ACM 49(2) show that the selfish equilibrium is at most 4/3 times worse than the social optimum. In this model the price of anarchy peaks at 1.33 (4/3) with 4,500 drivers (cost 0, sensitivity 10), equal to that bound.

You can verify with node tools/validate-braess.js. The simulation uses a seeded random generator (mulberry32), so the same seed gives the same result. The social optimum is the minimum average time found by trying every possible number of shortcut users one by one.

There is a fishery that everyone shares. If I catch a little more, I keep the gain alone while the cost of depletion is spread over everyone. Does everyone end up ruined, or can mutual monitoring and rules protect it? Follow the debate between Hardin and Ostrom with numbers.

That was a proposal tested in one university sample, and this page does not reproduce it.

Why Does the Bus Always Make You Wait Longer? · Simulatio Lab

If a bus comes every 10 minutes on average, why can you end up waiting 10 minutes on average? Run the waiting-time paradox (inspection paradox) and see why your class always feels more crowded than average.

"The bus is supposed to come every 10 minutes on average, so why do I always wait longer?" With a 10-minute average gap, showing up at a random moment should mean waiting 5 minutes on average. But if buses arrive unevenly, the average wait can be 10 minutes, not 5. It is not bad luck: a person who arrives at a random moment is more likely to land inside a long gap. Change how uneven the buses are, the average gap and the number of passengers, then check whether the same illusion explains why your class feels more crowded than the school average.

Buses come every average gap minutes, but the real gaps vary according to a gamma distribution. An irregularity (coefficient of variation = standard deviation of the gap ÷ mean) of 0 means a strict timetable, 1 means random arrivals, and larger values mean buses arrive in bunches.
Passengers do not know the timetable and arrive at any moment. The time until the next bus is the wait, and the bus gap they happened to land in is the gap the passenger saw.

A long gap takes up more room on the time axis, so the chance of a passenger landing in it is proportional to its length. That makes the average gap passengers see larger than the average gap you get by counting buses. The theory: average wait = average gap ÷ 2 × (1 + CV²).

The last panel applies the same calculation to class sizes. Counting classes one by one gives an average of 25, but if you ask students "how many are in your class?", students from big classes answer more often, so the average grows.

The "friendship paradox" (Scott Feld, 1991, American Journal of Sociology 96(6)), where your friends have more friends than you do, is the same sampling bias. There are five candidate societies. Each fixes an income for each of five positions (the population split into fifths by income; position 1 is the poorest). We assume that the more equal a society is, the lower its average income. That assumption drives the results.

A few words like "the", "of" and "and" make up a large part of any text, while most words almost never appear. Can this pile-up be produced not by what the words mean, but only by the habit of reusing what was already written?

The text is written one word at a time. With a small probability (the new-word probability) a brand-new word is invented; otherwise a word that already appeared is used again. The words are meaningless made-up ones (kia, marthiro, and so on).
Copy mode: copy the word at a random earlier position in the text. A word used often is scattered across the text, so it gets copied even more often (the rich get richer).
Uniform mode (the control): pick one of the distinct words seen so far with equal probability, no matter how often it has been used.

The result is viewed as a rank–frequency plot: rank the words from most to least used, put rank on the horizontal axis and the number of uses on the vertical axis, and draw both on log scales. Zipf's law then looks like a straight line with slope near -1.

This experiment only shows that "a single rich-get-richer rule can produce the same shape." The made-up words have no meaning, and neither grammar nor semantics is in the model.

Zipf (1949), Human Behavior and the Principle of Least Effort, made this regularity of word frequencies widely known. This is this project's own implementation, inspired by the "rich get richer" model of Simon (1955), "On a class of skew distribution functions", Biometrika 42 (new words appear occasionally and the rest is copied from the existing text; also known as the Yule–Simon process). It does not reproduce a figure from the paper.

The text is at most 100,000 words, and the slope is the log–log least-squares fit over ranks 3 to 200. At the default setting (3% new words) a 100,000-word text has about 3,000 distinct words, with the top 10 words covering about 85% of the text and the top 100 about 91% (6-text average).

In copy mode the slope had a size of 0.97 to 1.12 for new-word probabilities from 0.5% to 10%, near -1 (6-text average), while uniform choice gave 0.18 to 0.47, far shallower. Even in copy mode the value shifts a little with the fitting range and text length (1.26 for ranks 1–50, 1.09 for a 5,000-word text, 1.01 for a 100,000-word text).
